summary:
Perlis stands under Malaysia's federal Penal Code. Sections 377A and 377B punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and the Human Dignity Trust profile of Malaysia (updated 16 December 2025) records gross indecency offences alongside them. These federal provisions are not limited to Malaysian nationals and reach visitors, including in Perlis.

Perlis is one of all 13 states, together with Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, that maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences apply to Muslims only. Since the 1980s every state has passed such an enactment, three of them also bar women from posing as men. Enforcement sits with the state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, filed after the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Raid operations carry acute exposure risk, including for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among those held were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Human Rights Watch, with Justice For Sisters, reported on 10 August 2022 that state religious authorities had harassed LGBT activists and organisations and raided private events across the federation. The report, based on interviews with 73 LGBT people conducted across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, documents conversion practices including government-run "rehabilitation" programmes that at least 1,733 people had attended by June 2021.

The Human Dignity Trust profile records an enforcement pattern since the 2018 election: an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur in which at least 20 LGBT people were arrested, an August raid on an LGBT venue in which twenty men were arrested, a Terengganu Sharia court ordering a lesbian couple caned, and November 2023 plans in Johor for conversion-therapy centres. The same profile records that no legal gender-recognition procedure exists, that violence against LGBT people is regularly reported with transgender people particularly vulnerable, and that no anti-discrimination law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

No Perlis-specific enforcement case appears in the sources reviewed for this record. The national framework governs what a visitor faces in Perlis. For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, LGBT events and media content are censored, and there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, a figure corroborated by the Human Rights Watch count of programme attendance.

The two enforcement layers run on different tracks. The Sharia cross-dressing offences depend on religion and on state jurisdiction, so they have proved vulnerable in the Federal Court on federalism grounds, whereas the Penal Code offences apply to all persons regardless of religion and have not been narrowed by the same litigation.

Named cases in the sources come from other Malaysian states and the federal territories: Selangor and Kelantan provisions struck down, Johor conversion-centre plans, Terengganu caning of a lesbian couple, raids in Kuala Lumpur and Penang. They illustrate a federation-wide pattern rather than establishing a record of enforcement in Perlis itself.

Public exposure is a central mechanism of enforcement. Leaked detainee faces and personal details in the November 2025 Kuala Lumpur raid, pre-tipped media coverage, and suspension of identified civil servants indicate that arrest carries consequences beyond the criminal charge.

Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, which has no statutory definition of transgender dressing to work from.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in Malaysia, so there is no procedure by which a resident in Perlis can obtain documents matching their gender identity. outOfScopeNotes:
No Perlis-specific enforcement case, arrest figure, or raid record appears in the sources reviewed for this state; the national framework is what the sources support here, and Perlis's own implementation of its Sharia enactment is not documented.

Three Malaysian states also bar women from posing as men, but the sources do not name them; whether Perlis is among them is unresolved.

Whether Perlis operates mukhayyam retreats, conversion-therapy centres, or a dedicated religious-department enforcement unit against transgender people is not sourced.

The current status of the 2014 constitutional challenge to the cross-dressing prohibition after the Federal Court's 2021 and 2024 federalism rulings is unresolved on this inventory; the sources confirm only that the High Court declined the declaration and that the rulings left the federal offences intact.

The sources do not state whether Perlis's cross-dressing provision is worded differently from those of other states, nor whether caning as a sentence has been imposed in Perlis specifically.
